item.content:encoded:
Cosy nooks and a study are among the spaces designed for reading at House of Shadows, a multi-generational home in Bengaluru, Karnataka, by Indian studio Cadence Architects.

Located on a quiet, tree-lined road, the house was designed for a family of bookworms who moved back to India after living in the USA for over a decade.

Cadence Architects utilised a predominantly dark, shadowy material palette for the home and fronted it with slatted screens, designed to create a feeling of seclusion and privacy.

"The client, with his young family of two children, was moving back from the USA after having stayed there for 15 years," principal architect Smaran Mallesh told Dezeen.

"As a family of readers, they wanted their home to be a repository for their books and conducive to reading," he continued.

"He wanted to build this home where he could also have his parents come and live with him."

Outside, the home is distinguished by its dark material palette, including a basalt stone base and concrete walls and a roof. A slatted timber facade screens the living spaces while allowing light and air to filter in.

According to the studio, the dark materials were all chosen for their robustness and to help the home blend with "the shadows of the trees and make the home less conspicuous on the street".

Inside, the House of Shadow's spatial organisation is intended to cater for the preferences and needs of the three generations that live there. The ground level of the home has a kitchen, living and dining area for entertaining guests.

Private living spaces for the grandparents are also on this floor.

Above, the first floor is for the parents and their children, complete with a study and reading nooks.

Described by the studio as the "more secluded and introspective" level, it was intended to offer the feeling of a quiet retreat.

Read:

Multi-generational LJ House in Ahmedabad prioritises shared living

"Books and reading spaces form an important part of the interiors, encouraging the family to pause, read, and linger," the studio said.

The third level is given over to an entertainment area for the children to enjoy with their friends. The home is complete with various terraces, decks and balconies that help keep the interiors cool.

Inside, Cadence Architects contrasted the darkness of the exterior with lighter shades through a mix of natural and local materials such as wood and lime plaster.

However, darker shades were still used in more intimate spaces, such as the reading nooks, to add a feeling of cosiness.

"We wanted to make a home that is crafted locally, with local materials," said Mallesh.

"It was important to do that for a client who is moving back and seeking his roots, in a sense. However, we were not interested in the vernacular per se but wanted a modern rendition of these traditional techniques of making."

Other multigenerational Indian houses recently featured on Dezeen include LJ House in Ahmedabad, which Studio Saransh and Iksoi Studio designed with gently curving rooflines and an asymmetrical heart-shaped stairwell, and Splitscape Residence in Coimbatore, which SpaceDNA organised around a triple-height void with an oxide-coated staircase.

The photography is by Syam Sreesylam.

item.content:encoded:
Bamboo-clad parasols and a three-storey bamboo truss feature in this roundup of buildings from Southeast and South Asia built using the fast-growing plant.

Mahamudra Meditation Centre, Nepal, by Abari

A mandala-shaped bamboo truss crowns this Buddhist meditation centre in Tibet, Nepal, which is perched atop a mountain near the country's capital, Kathmandu.

Designed by architecture studio Abari, the centre contains a main hall, with a three-tiered structure that houses a 15-metre-tall meditation space, alongside a dining hall and guest house.

Find out more about the Mahamudra Meditation Centre ›

Tapmi Centre, India, by The Purple Ink Studio

Local practice The Purple Ink Studio used a canopy of parasols clad in bamboo to shelter the social hub of this business school in southwest India.

Designed to challenge conventional academic buildings, the space is organised around a sunken amphitheatre and provides a communal hub for the school's 30,000 students.

Find out more about Tapmi Centre ›

Living Bridge, Indonesia, by Jonathon Mizzi

Architect Jonathan Mizzi collaborated with students to create Living Bridge, a learning centre for a school in Indonesia.

Built from more than 300 pieces of heat-bent bamboo, the building provides a flexible space for hosting events and talks, which is partially open to the elements.

Find out more about Living Bridge ›

Chicken Hero Pavilion, Indonesia, by RAD+ar

An artificial hill was used to disguise a bamboo chicken coop, which was temporarily added to a park in Jakarta, Indonesia.

Completed by Balinese architecture studio RAD+ar, the structure was built from a bamboo lattice supported by a series of bamboo and steel columns designed as a prototype for a low-impact chicken coop.

Find out more about Chicken Hero Pavilion ›

Intaaya Retreat, Indonesia, by Pablo Luna Studio

Balinese practice Pablo Luna Studio drew on seashells, fish and manta rays for the undulating bamboo roofs of this wellness retreat in Indonesia.

Situated on the edge of a cliff on the island Nusa Penida, the retreat comprises 12 guest suites alongside a yoga studio, spa, restaurant and tea room.

Find out more about Intaaya Retreat ›

The Juliet Centre, Pakistan, by Jack Rankin and Nyami Studio

A vaulted bamboo structure frames this community workshop and event space in Pakistan, completed by Northern Irish architect Jack Rankin and UK practice Nyami Studio.

Located in Pono Village, a settlement originally developed by the Heritage Foundation of Pakistan and its founder, Yasmeen Lari, The Juliet Centre serves as a pilot scheme for zero-carbon flood-resilient homes.

Find out more about The Juliet Centre ›

Anjung, Malaysia,  by Eleena Jamil

Malaysian architect Eleena Jamil used a bamboo and green-painted steel canopy to shade this house and studio space near Kuala Lumpur.

Named Anjung, the project comprises two single-storey buildings containing a four-bedroom guesthouse in one and a small workspace in the other.

Find out more about Anjung ›

item.content:encoded:
Danish design brand Fritz Hansen has teamed up with audio specialist Technics to transform its Farringdon showroom into a series of domestic listening scenes for London Design Festival.

As part of the Fritz Hansen Sound Club, the showroom has been organised into four domestic scenes where guests are invited to listen to a curated selection of vinyl records.

The installation combines Fritz Hansen's furniture and lighting products with turntables, headphones and speakers from Japanese firm Technics.

A 90th anniversary limited edition of the Kaiser Idell Luxus table lamp and Technics' SL 40CBT turntable form the centrepiece of the various settings, both reimagined in a matching burgundy hue.

In reference to the table lamp's modernist origins, the interior styling evokes the Bauhaus movement and combines 1930s furniture with pieces from Fritz Hansen's catalogue.

Fritz Hansen Sound Club originally debuted during 3 Days of Design in Copenhagen, with the aim to explore how sound informs the way users experience interior settings.

,"Sound plays a direct role in how we experience space," said Fritz Hansen creative director, Els Van Hoorebeeck. "It shapes how we move, where we pause, and how we relate to furniture, light and materials."

"With Fritz Hansen Sound Club, we explore how these elements work together to define the character of a space, and how this way of thinking continues to shape our design today."

Read:

London design "an international success story" says Sadiq Khan

The Study area pairs steel-framed desks with Arne Jacobsen's Ant Chair in a cherry veneer finish, while the designer's iconic Egg Chair provides a cosy spot for relaxing in the nearby Reading Corner.

Downstairs, the Living Room provides a setting for socialising, with a turntable and speakers oriented towards the guests.

Furniture including Poul Kjærholm's PK31 sofa and PK80 daybed creates a relaxed, lounge-like feel, while a 1930s drinks trolley and PK61 coffee tables encourage conversation and interaction.

Fritz Hansen was founded in 1872 and is known for working with famous architects and designers, including Jacobsen and Kjærholm, as well as Hans J Wegner, Børge Mogensen and Verner Panton.

More recently, the brand has collaborated with contemporary talents such as Piero Lissoni, Jamie Hayon and Cecilie Manz, who created a compact and comfortable plywood chair that can be used in a variety of contexts.

A new version of Manz's Monolit chair forms part of the presentation, alongside a more compact, wall-mounted take on the Kaiser Idell lamp and an upholstered version of Japanese studio Nendo's N02 Recycle chair.

Other highlights from this year's London Design Festival include the debut show of design platform Collate Lobby and a bamboo pavilion covered in traditional Indian police shields.

Fritz Hansen Sound Club is open daily to the public until 20 September at 78 Cowcross Street as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian designer Victoria Yakusha has created a sculptural, almost monochromatic interior for a jewellery brand's flagship boutique in New York City.

Also from Ukraine, the brand Guzema's store in SoHo is its first US flagship and occupies a 1,100-square-foot (102-square-metre) space on Wooster Street.

Victoria Yakusha Studio used her signature minimalist style to design a space that feels calming and curated.

"My work here was closer to that of a sculptor," said founder Victoria Yakusha. "We didn't want the feeling of traditional retail. We wanted something more intimate."

The long, narrow interior is laid out with products presented in recessed niches on both sides, and inside a series of sculptural vitrines running back through the centre.

These monolithic islands are upholstered in dove-grey suede and "rounded like a river stone" to create a soft, serene statement.

The remainder of the decor is slightly lighter in colour, with mineral-toned plaster and matching storage units creating the impression of a single cohesive surface.

In the store window, a series of white hand-sculpted vessels with textured skins and bowl-like tops are used to present Guzema's jewellery in a novel way.

Read:

Victoria Yakusha opens Miami gallery with plant-covered "living island"

These pieces follow the same visual language as the Sonaih floor lamp from Yakusha's own design brand Faina, which produces furniture, lighting and decor.

"We wanted the jewelry to feel discovered, not just displayed. That's how we came to the idea of the installation," Yakusha said. "Each vessel is hand-sculpted, layer by layer. It's an artwork in itself. It becomes part of the experience, a way of revealing something precious."

At the back of the store is a semi-private consultation area for one-on-one appointments, screened from the main space by a glass-block partition.

Several more Faina designs feature in this salon, including a curved sofa, ottoman and sconce, along with a burnished-metal table and silver tableware by Natalia Criado.

A former fashion editor, Yakusha has opened galleries for her furniture line in both Antwerp and Miami, and earlier designed the interior for Kyiv eatery Istetyka that balances rough and smooth surfaces.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, she has designed a furniture collection as an homage to her homeland and proposed a museum to preserve threatened Ukrainian cultural heritage.

The photography is by Matthew Williams.

item.content:encoded:
A green-concrete frontage marks the transformation of a neglected building in Hastings into Eagle House community centre, designed by London architecture studio IF_DO.

Eagle House was completed for community-led developer Hastings Commons and provides a mixture of public space, work areas and youth facilities.

Rather than demolish and replace the neglected Victorian building, IF_DO looked to turn it back into an active "part of the street", onto which a ground floor common room can open via large, openable windows framed by a green-concrete frontage.

"What we were really designing was civic infrastructure, a building that could hold a free community room, affordable workspace and dedicated youth facilities all at once, and do so in a way that felt genuinely welcoming rather than institutional," IF_DO co-founder Sarah Castle told Dezeen.

"Large operable windows set within deep recesses mean that people inside the common room can quite literally sit at the window and have a conversation with someone waiting for the bus outside," she added.

"The building stops being a container and becomes part of the street. In a town where many people, particularly young people, can feel invisible, that matters."

The common room of Eagle House is spread across its ground and lower ground floors. The upper area is framed in bright canary-yellow steelwork and features sit-in timber window boxes overlooking the street.

Above, three storeys of flexible, affordable work areas and counselling spaces for young people are organised around a new circulation core. This contains a lift and a repositioned, skylit staircase, also painted canary yellow.

Read:

Thing converts historic Cornish library into The Ladder arts space

The bold colour palette – chosen through sessions with members of Hastings Commons' youth organisation – continues through the building as a wayfinding strategy, with pink doorframes and walls in shades of orange, blue and green.

These colourful painted surfaces sit alongside exposed services and ducting, wood-wool wall panels and sisal flooring, keeping the spaces deliberately simple and easy to maintain while also providing acoustic comfort.

In the attic, the ceiling has been clad in timber reclaimed from the building's external walls, which have been re-rendered in pale lime, with subtly textured finishes around the windows and parapet.

"It was important that those uses were not just stacked on top of each other but genuinely connected, spatially and socially. The building needed to feel like one thing, not a collection of separate tenants," Castle said.

"We wanted the materials to feel honest and durable, things that would age well and that the community could understand and own," she added.

Elsewhere in the UK, architecture studio Thing recently converted a historic library and college in Cornwall into a community arts and culture hub, contrasting exposed, worn surfaces with new additions in timber.

Architecture collective Assemble recently converted a pair of former dairy warehouses into a community centre and church in east London.

The photography is by Killian O'Sullivan.

item.content:encoded:
Our latest roundup collects houses topped with verdant green roofs, with some designed to blend into the natural landscape and others providing elevated garden space for families to gather.

A green roof is a roof covered in vegetation that grows over a waterproof membrane and is designed to help absorb rainwater, improve insulation in the building and add wildlife to the site.

The examples below show how green roofs can be added to homes in clever ways, disguising them in their surroundings and giving residents a connection to the outdoors.

Earth, Japan, by Sou Fujimoto

Designed by Japanese architect Sou Fujimoto for hotelier Not A Hotel, this curved holiday home blends into the landscape with a garden space that rises over the rooftop from ground level.

Situated on Ishigaki Island, Japan, an oval-shaped terrace cuts into the sloping garden and leads to a living and dining room, which open onto an infinity pool and curved terrace on the other side.

Find out more about Earth ›

Forest House, Argentina, by Gonzalo Bardach Arquitectura

A ramping green roof rises over Forest House, a concrete woodland house near the coast outside Buenos Aires that was designed by local studio Gonzalo Bardach Arquitectura.

Gonzalo Bardach Arquitectura nestled the residence into a dune, creating a connection between indoor and outdoor spaces with framed views that cut through the uneven topography.

Find out more about Forest House ›

Split Mass Residence, Indonesia, by K-Thengono Design Studio

In Tangerang, Indonesia, local firm K-Thengono Design Studio created a three-storey home with sloping green roofs connecting indoor living spaces with the outdoors.

Wrapped in PE rattan facades, the house has a grassy outdoor staircase that leads residents from an open-plan kitchen, living and dining room to the swimming pool and barbecue area above.

Find out more about Split Mass Residence ›

The Inside Home, Iran, by Olgoo

The Inside Home is a subterranean holiday home in the village of Ammameh near Tehran, which Iranian architecture studio Olgoo designed in response to rapid development and loss of green spaces in the area.

Pentagonal in plan, the home is made up of three concrete blocks arranged around a central courtyard, with planting populating the roof overhead.

Find out more about The Inside Home ›

Ashraya, UK, by Kirkland Fraser Moor

A curving green roof supported by a cross-laminated timber arch soars over Ashraya, a home located in the Chiltern Hills Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty in Hertfordshire.

Bookended by two semicircular sunken courtyards, UK studio Kirkland Fraser Moor designed the two-storey house to be a contemporary addition to the landscape while also blending into the natural scenery.

Find out more about Ashraya ›

Villa Aa, Norway, by CF Møller Architects

Danish studio CF Møller Architects nestled this concrete villa into a shallow hill on a Norwegian farm, hiding it from view as people approach by disguising it under the low green roof.

Two sweeping ramps cut into the green roof to form entrances on either side of the home, skylights dot the roof to illuminate the interior and outdoor terraces overlook the nearby Oslofjord.

Find out more about Villa Aa ›

Landaburu Borda, Spain, by Jordi Hidalgo Tané

A glass corridor connects a small stone building to a subterranean green-roofed annex designed by architecture studio Jordi Hidalgo Tané.

Located in rural Navarra, Spain, Jordi Hidalgo Tané hid the concrete extension under the adjacent hillside, aiming to not disrupt the picturesque natural setting.

Find out more about Landaburu Borda ›

Forest House, Thailand, by Shma Company

Aiming to squeeze in as much greenery as possible, landscape architecture practice Shma Company planted 20 species of flora in 300 square metres of space at Forest House in Bangkok.

Accommodating seven people and 120 trees, the house is made up of three white volumes that were arranged to form two courtyards and multiple green roofs.

Find out more about Forest House ›

item.content:encoded:
This week on Dezeen, we looked at the highlights of this week's London Design Festival, which included a pavilion topped with police shields.

Built on The Strand, in central London, The Pangolin Shield pavilion (pictured) has a bamboo structure topped with two types of shield – traditional Indian police shields constructed out of lathis and woven rain shields called knups.

To coincide with London Design Festival (LDF) we created an issue of Dezeen Dispatch, which was distributed at sites across the city and is available to read online here.

Highlights of LDF included the One Tool Stool exhibition by students from the Royal College of Art and a fictional 1930s hotel suite created as the backdrop for the first editions collection by new design platform Lobby.

In a Q&A with Sadiq Khan in Dezeen Dispatch, the mayor of London described the city's design as "an international success story".

Following last week's launch of Dyson's first toothbrush, we looked back at four products that the brand successfully revolutionised, and four it didn't.

Successes include vacuums, fans, hand driers and hair care products.

In architecture news, Hotelier Not A Hotel unveiled its latest unusual guesthouse – a human-sized Pokémon Poké Ball.

Set to be nestled beside a lake in Hokkaido, Japan, the three-metre-diameter spherical guest room swill be shaped like the balls used to catch creatures in the popular Pokémon game.

Reporting from Helsinki Design Week we looked at the story behind a Matti Suuronen Futuro House that has been manufactured for the first time in decades.

The creation of the house, which was on display at the festival, began when architect Jan van Dijs was made aware of an unusual post on Facebook by a friend and client.

Popular projects this week included the Pine House holiday home in southern Sweden by Johan Sundberg Arkitektur, a wooden cabin "devoted entirely to the ritual of bathing" in the UK and a "strong yet subtle" cottage extension in Scotland.

Listen to our journalists talk about the key design and architecture stories of the past seven days on our Dezeen Weekly podcast, which this week focused on London Design Festival.

item.content:encoded:
New York creative agency Basura and musician Big Data have collaborated on a stuffed toy that resembles a data centre and emits a recording from a data centre in Virginia when squeezed.

The stuffed toy, called Bezzy, is part of a larger satirical campaign that draws attention to the impact of data centres and AI as part of the launch of Big Data's first album in over seven years.

Basura founder Rajeev Basu said the team interviewed "dozens" of people living near data centres for the project and eventually shaped it into the Adopt a Data Centre campaign that includes a website, stickers, posters and Bezzy.

Overall, it imagines "AI data centers as rescue animals looking for their forever homes" according to Basura, informed by initiatives such as WWF's Adopt-a-Panda.

Basu said the toy and campaign were meant to show the absurdity of the data centre building boom, driven by AI, which has led to noise complaints from communities near the functioning data centres.

"Adopt A Data Center is an absurd and provocative invitation to look more closely at what we're being asked to welcome into our lives," Basu told Dezeen. 

Read:

First images of Gensler-designed 60-building data centre development in Utah revealed

The toy is handmade, with a soft body that depicts a data centre, a smile, eyes, and long legs and arms.

When it's squeezed, it emits a recording taken by one of the team's interviewees, a woman who lives by a data centre in Virginia.

"Hug me for ear piercing forever hum," reads a tag on Bezzy.

Basu said the interviews were prompted by the desire to understand what living near a data centre "actually feels like".

"The experiences varied, but the same concerns kept coming up: noise, light, changes to the land use and implications for local residents, and demands on local water and electricity," he said.

There are a total of 20 Bezzy toys as part of the release of Big Data's EP 4.0.

The team said the project is "not anti-AI, or anti-technology" but rather seeks to prompt questions about how AI is used responsibly.

"When the promises are so enormous, from transforming everyday life to shaping the future of humanity, the commitment to safety and accountability needs to be just as substantial," said Basu.

Massive data centres are currently being built around the world to support AI models and use large amounts of energy and water on top of the massive land usage. A recently announced hyperscale data centre for AI in Utah will have as much as 10,000 acres dedicated to the facilities.

Recently, residents from around Memphis, Tennessee, sued businessman Elon Musk over the noise pollution, reported NPR.

And beyond sound, scientists have released preliminary studies that point to a pronounced heat island effect as a result of data centre development.

The images are courtesy Basura

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a housing project for victims of domestic violence with courtyards, winter gardens and a nursery is among architecture projects by Cardiff University students.

Also featured is a pottery workshop that uses materials found in the River Taff and a weather archive and artist residency in the Preseli Hills.

Cardiff University

Institution: Cardiff University
School: Welsh School of Architecture
Course: BSc Architecture
Tutor: Aled Davies

School statement:

"The Welsh School of Architecture (WSA), based in Cardiff, is a world-renowned institution for design and built environment studies.

"Originally founded over a century ago, the WSA has a strong tradition of excellence in architectural education.

"Our teaching and research embrace the diversity and transdisciplinary nature of architecture – we foster curious, creative, critical, ethical learners who can approach challenges with wide-ranging, flexible skills and knowledge.

"Our vision is to contribute to the making of built environments that enhance the wellbeing of current and future generations while caring for the planet.

"The BSc in Architecture is a three-year undergraduate degree course accredited by RIBA, ARB and LAM (Malaysia).

"The programme covers design, technology, history, theory, representation and professional practice dimensions of the architectural discipline.

"Through studio projects, we encourage our students to take a holistic view of how buildings are designed, used, made and what their broader impacts are, whilst fostering an ethos of 'grounded creativity', exposing students to real-world sites and live challenges as the basis for design projects.

"These approaches are reflected in the range of our year three design units, each of which empowers students to explore and tackle pressing issues for architecture, cities and society."

Managing Pollution Through Making Art by Thomas Brownlie

"The project addresses the heavy metal pollution present in the River Taff caused by historical mining and ongoing industrial activity.

"It proposes the creation of a public workshop and material sourcing space dedicated to the ceramic ash glazing process.

"An ecosystem of phyto-remediating plants will be established to extract heavy metals from the river and surrounding soil.

"Once harvested, these plants will be burned, and their ash used in ceramic glazes.

"By transforming contaminated material into a resource for pottery, the project supports local artistic practice while encouraging public engagement with environmental remediation, craft and material experimentation."

Student: Thomas Brownlie
Tutor: Aled Davies
Email: brownlie.thomas1[at]gmail.com

Social Brewery Development Project, Re-vitalising the Community of Rhos-y-Bwlch (Rosebush) by Annest Marian Davies

"Using primary systems of labour(field) and gathering(forest), this project proposes a national-scale brewery alongside civic infrastructure for the town of Rosebush, Pembrokeshire.

"Seeking to address the forgotten condition of rural Welsh villages, research is built atop former participatory economic systems in mining communities, studying how social mobility was facilitated through the reaping of a stable core industry, pooling wealth back into the local area.

"Through integrating the scheme alongside Pembrokeshire's modern renewable industries, the brewery project aims to revitalise the area both socially and economically, designing for the future while maintaining a deep consideration of existing fabric."

Student: Annest Marian Davies
Tutor: William Beeston
Email: annestmd[at]gmail.com

Tywydd a Thir (Weather and Land) by Sabah Humayun

"Tywydd a Thir is a weather archive and artist residency situated within the mythical, unpredictable landscape of the Preseli Hills, where shifting skies, ancient stone alignments and ever-changing climatic conditions become the project's primary design drivers.

"Rather than sheltering occupants from the elements, the architecture embraces weather as a living force, allowing wind, rain, fog and light to shape movement, perception and memory.

"Embedded within the landscape through rammed earth, stone, and weathering materials, the building evolves alongside its surroundings, becoming part of the site's geological and cultural narrative.

"The project reimagines architecture as an instrument for observing, recording, and experiencing the unforecastable character of place through atmosphere and time."

Student: Sabah Humayun
Tutors: Will Beeston, Parvathy Vipulendran and Varun Nambiar
Email: sabah.humayun[at]outlook.com

Re-Quarter; A Catalytic Social Housing Scheme by Isaac Walker

"Inequality isn't always visible: architecture and urbanism dictate our physical environment, affecting how we live, work and survive.

"Stokes Croft, in Bristol, exhibits an attractive and functional urban space, yet fails a vulnerable population, with 1,720 cases of violent and sexual offences in three years.

"This housing project seeks to provide housing for victims of domestic violence, utilising feminist theory and trauma-informed design.

"An active ground plan provides employment, childcare, therapy and greenspace – a confident plinth for the housing to reside on.

"With courtyards, winter gardens, a nursery and varied housing units, the scheme explores how architecture can be catalytic."

item.content:encoded:
A group of five New York artists has created Lifeline, a tote bag that can convert into a self-inflating life jacket as a conceptual design object meant to bring awareness to the threat of climate change-related flooding.

Timed to New York Climate Week, the as-yet-unnamed group used a standard nylon life jacket to create the object, which is meant to be conceptual and is not for sale.

Driven by the recent flooding in the New York City subway system, Lifeline was designed to be a commentary on consumer fashion and on the emergencies of climate change by contrasting the everyday design of a functional tote bag with the emergency design of a life jacket.

Central to the commentary is the absurdity that such an item needs to exist, or makes sense in context.

"The overarching principle for this project is an essential that shouldn't exist," group member and creative director Phil Le Brun told Dezeen.

"It's an inquiry into conditions and the world which gave rise to this object."

According to designer Gabriela Mestriner, who worked on the project, the final product includes three yards of nylon, polyester zippers, cording and metal locks, most of which came from a deconstructed life vest.

The material was then heat-welded back together.

A zipper that runs through the centre of the bag flap and through the body opens to allow for a person's head to pass through. The set up includes a detached rain hood that can be stored in the bag.

Similar to a regular life jacket, the Lifeline is inflated by pulling on straps. Le Brun said that in testing, they were able to pull off the conversion from tote bag to life jacket in around 15 seconds.

Important to the project was what Le Brun calls the "language of emergency" seen in the orange of the final and the inflation mechanism.

However, the styling and photoshoot around the design also helped in the communication of the concept behind the design, with the group working to present the bag in photography that appears almost glamorous.

Le Brun said that they were aware of this perception and wanted to lean into it.

"The contrast of normality and then emergency, that juxtaposition and that friction, was deliberate," he said. "It was a deliberate choice for the bag to look kind of cool and normal and be actually functional."

The fact that the life jacket is "hidden" within the bag is a direct commentary on what the group sees as the negative effects of consumerism.

"Hidden within our style and our fashion and our consumerism is a fucking emergency," Le Brun said.

Read:

Tian & Teague creates home decor informed by the "discomforts" of New York

On the other hand, the photoshoot features images of the bag being converted into a life jacket in the subway, an eerie look into its potential usefulness.

When asked how the message of the design would impact people, Le Brun emphasised the media around it as an important aspect of getting the point across and called it a "narrative object".

"I like to think of it as a narrative object," he said. "I want it to be something that sparks people to think about the choices they make."

Lifeline is the group's debut concept and Le Brun said they hope to continue exploring ideas through design.

Other conceptual designs include the Bliss Couch, which creative agency Mother made to function as a life raft.

In Sweden, developer Riksbyggen and creative agency BBDO Nordics created scale apartments based on what young people can afford to highlight the country's housing unaffordability.

item.content:encoded:
A sculptural cluster of cylindrical forms defines the "calm, continuous" House in Las Rozas, a home in Madrid completed by local studio Fran Silvestre Arquitectos.

Overlooking the Sierra de Guadarrama on the outskirts of Madrid, the home's cylindrical volumes emerge from a gently sloping site and are finished in crisp white render with sloping roofs.

This design gives rise to what Fran Silvestre Arquitectos described as "geometric clarity".

"We were interested in exploring how a very simple operation could generate an architecture that is precise and recognisable, while remaining completely connected to its use and context," said studio founder Fran Silvestre.

"The choice of materials responds to the intention of reinforcing the geometric clarity of the project and creating a calm, continuous architecture," he added.

"The result may appear different from other houses designed by the studio, but it responds to the same principles that underpin our work – precision, economy of means and the pursuit of maximum spatial intensity with the fewest possible elements."

House in Las Rozas's three largest cylinders contain living spaces across a single floor. In each, a central, orthogonal arrangement of rooms is flanked by two semicircular terraces, some covered and others left open to the elements.

The exterior's minimalist finishes continue throughout the interiors, with plain, curving walls emphasising the movement of sunlight, complemented by pale stone floors and bespoke white storage.

Read:

Stepped volumes create panoramic terraces for Villa 95 by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos

"We sought a restrained material palette capable of highlighting light, shadow and the perception of the curved surfaces without competing with them," said Silvestre.

"Rather than working with a wide variety of finishes, we are interested in reducing the number of elements and allowing geometry, light and the passage of time to construct the atmosphere."

Where the three cylindrical living volumes meet at the home's centre is a small, triangular courtyard – a sculptural space squeezed between high, convex walls.

"The courtyard brings together many of the project's central ideas – geometry, light, intimacy and the way architecture can transform our perception of space," Silvestre explained.

Alongside the home, an additional smaller cylinder contains an elevated swimming pool and terrace, accessible from the terraces of the living, dining and kitchen area and bedrooms through full-height sliding glass doors.

Silvestre founded his eponymous practice in 2005. Previous projects by the studio include a home in Andalusia formed of volumes that zigzag up a sloping plot and the glazed Hoffman House, which is topped by a dramatic T-shaped roof.

The photography is by Fernando Guerra.

item.content:encoded:
Chinese designer Bin Wu has unveiled the Pavilion of Time, which features timber screens topped by a circular mirror, in the courtyard of Domaine National du Palais-Royal for Paris Design Week.

Wu described the pavilion, which he created in response to the theme of this year's Paris Design Week, Pulse in Motion, as "making time tangible and walkable".

Beneath its circular roof, the pavilion is divided into three timber segments, each of which has an opening to allow visitors to walk through them in a circle.

Wu wrapped the timber structure in a translucent, paper‑like membrane to allow natural sunlight into the structure and let visitors perceive the movement of time through the shifting light.

"We hope people move continuously – footsteps trace the arc, sunlight drifts through paper and mirror, wandering between ground and structure," Wu said.

"Light and shadow become intangible hands, inscribing time's trajectory. Here, time is measured not by clocks, but by light; not in numbers, but through the body's motion and repose."

According to Wu, the circular form of the pavilion was designed to contrast the orthogonal classical architecture of the Domaine National du Palais-Royal, while also referencing the ancient Chinese concept of "a round heaven and a square earth".

Its light, translucent design was also deliberately created in juxtaposition to the perceived heaviness of the surrounding historical architecture.

The paper-like membrane that covers the pavilion is made of polyethylene, suitable for outdoor use and resembles the texture of traditional Chinese Xuan paper.

Read:

Uchronia installs giant floral sculpture at Grand Palais for Paris Design Week

Wu used products from Chinese brands for the pavilion, including a lighting system developed by Chinese smart home brand Moorgen.

This casts a soft light through the translucent walls and allows the pavilion to be lit up at night.

Carbon fibre chairs from Chinese furniture brand Shang Xia were placed at the outer edges of the pavilion, inviting visitors to pause and rest.

Overall, Wu aimed for the pavilion to give visitors an insight into an Eastern way of experiencing time.

"Eastern time is not a straight line, but a series of perceivable moments," Wu said.

"The Pavilion of Time takes this as its impetus, combining Chinese painting's shifting perspective and temporality to let the body perceive spatial and temporal change."

Wu is the founder of interior studio W Design, which was recognised as interior designer of the year at Dezeen Awards China 2024.

He recently published a book titled The Design Language of Timeless East, exploring the idea of a design language rooted in the philosophical context of the East.

Elsewhere at Paris Design Week, French design studio Uchronia designed a giant floral sculpture at Grand Palais museum.

The photography is by SHIDAI.

item.content:encoded:
From laser-cut steel to melted polystyrene waste, 10 designers have reinterpreted the humble hanging basket for a London Design Festival exhibition curated by design gallery Slancha.

Dangling chains and elaborate 3D-printed cups also feature among the 10 hanging baskets displayed in the Hackney studio of fashion agency and retailer Awaykin.

The brief set by Slancha founders Harvey Everson and Findlay MacDonald was to reconsider the hanging basket – a suspended planter typically used for growing flowers – as a collectable design object.

"We invited 10 contemporary designers to work from the same loose framework of bracket, suspension and vessel, interpreting it through their own materials and practices," MacDonald told Dezeen.

"We selected designers that work across a range of materials, so we knew that the outcomes would all be completely different," he continued.

"It means we have all ends of the spectrum in the show, from really beautiful, small, refined pieces, to larger, more grotesque ones that are somehow beautiful and ugly at the same time."

Among the more abnormal pieces is Pyrofoam Planter by French designer Nicolas Zanoni, a wall-hung basket made by melting industrial polystyrene waste so that it takes on an organic, caramelised form.

Another is Tri-diatreta by London-based Coline Le Quenven, a steel armature that supports three 3D-printed cups, combining references that include Roman cage cups and the neo-Greek bronze furniture of France's Villa Kérylos.

"It's so close to what a traditional hanging basket bracket would be like, but then there's the use of 3D printing, which creates these incredible patterns on the outside," said MacDonald.

Romain Basile Petrot was one of three designers to put a twist on a single suspended basket, using stacked plates of aluminium engraved with the lyrics of David Bowie's Space Oddity.

Marc Sweeney paired a recycled champagne bucket from his Pylon series with a fine stainless-steel ball chain, while Martha McGuinn of Jamps Studio used laser cutting to recreate forms found in medieval manuscripts and gothic architecture.

Hanna Fastrich pushed the brief the most in her brutalism-inspired design, Red Hot, a cantilevered arrangement of two slab-built ceramic blocks with a deep red glaze and a small conical dish for flowers.

"The texture is incredible; it almost looks like the bark of a tree," suggested MacDonald.

The smallest works come from Six Dots Design and ThisIsByron, who both created tubular aluminium forms, while Sheyang Li created a larger but more delicate piece featuring an ash wood hook, a stone support, an aluminium tube and a suspended ceramic vase.

Completing the series is a design by London studio All Ears. It features four vases held inside a striped wooden block, made from alternating layers of maple and walnut, while chains hang down like stems.

The baskets were styled with floral arrangements by Glasgow-based Studio Kumari, featuring dark purple lilies, thistles and yellow tomatoes.

Slancha was recently named on Dezeen as one of five galleries injecting renewed energy into the London design scene.

This show comes a year after the Scottish duo presented the LDF exhibition, The Car Boot Sale, which established their reputation.

MacDonald said the duo felt the best way to follow up the success was to do something completely different this year. In addition to Hanging Baskets, the pair have also created an exhibition and a curated pop-up shop at The Hoxton hotel.

"We were quite nervous to come back this year, because we knew everything was going to be a comparison to last year," he said. "We wanted something incomparable to last year, but equally fun in its narrative."

The photography is courtesy of Slancha.

Dezeen Showroom: Finnish company Khoy's flagship product transforms from a seat into a bed by simply unzipping it, without relying on conventional "over-engineered" mechanisms.

Available in sizes ranging from single to king, the Khoy sofa bed is made of two simple slabs of polyurethane foam that fold open like a book to make an expansive floor bed.

Inspired by the sofas of the 1970s, the bed is designed to deliver genuine comfort – whether for residents lounging at home or guests sleeping overnight – while simplifying the look and feel.

"Traditional sofa beds are often either uncomfortable as sofas, uncomfortable as beds, or both," said Khoy. "They can also be heavy, over-engineered and aesthetically compromised by the mechanisms needed to make them multifunctional."

"Khoy takes a different approach: remove the unnecessary complexity and make comfort the starting point."

Khoy was also the first company in this space to ship its sofas vacuum packed, reducing their volume for easier handling and distribution.

The sofas can be ordered with optional frames to support them if positioned away from a wall and are available in a choice of 12 fabrics.

Chiselled acoustic foam, hand-bent metal and interlocking rulers feature in an exhibition of stools created with single tools, presented by students from the Royal College of Art at London Design Festival.

One Tool, One Stool is the culmination of an exercise undertaken by every design products master's student at the Royal College of Art (RCA).

As the exhibition title suggests, each student was challenged to conceive a stool using a single tool and minimal materials.

Twenty-three of the varied results are on display at The Lavery in South Kensington, arranged across the floor like precious artefacts within the workspace of the venue's namesake, the late painter John Lavery.

Ranging from practical to more abstract examples, each stool features a different design. Among the pieces is a low-slung seat by Sue Ye, formed from orange and yellow paint rollers strung together with thin red rope.

Close by is a dusty pink stool by Pil Gyu Jan, made of slabs of acoustic foam that were subtly chiselled into shape.

Mayank Patole has crafted a simple, eight-pronged stool out of 10 stainless steel 6o-centimetre rulers. The experimental stool is held together by a single nut and bolt and was created to highlight how a set of measuring tools can become a load-bearing structure.

Considering the exhibition concept, the RCA said, "the exercise asks students to consider how much can be achieved with very little, encouraging resourcefulness and a direct relationship between thinking and making".

"Each response reveals a different approach to materials, construction and problem-solving," added the university.

Elsewhere in the exhibition, Anisa Yelek is presenting a bulbous stool made from a cluster of white candles melded together using a heat gun.

Read:

Collate Lobby curates fictional 1930s hotel suite to launch its first editions collection

Yelek wanted to create seating that encouraged quiet contemplation.

"It's a stool that might melt," she said. "It's a seat that asks you to think about what it means to sit, to stay, to burn."

Nymph Mongkolcheep has designed a textured, cubic stool wreathed in wooden beads bound by spindly wire.

Next to Mongkolcheep's piece, Vincent Schwarz placed a hand-bent piece of metal that was shaped to provide seating – among the most minimalist stools in the show.

One Tool, One Stool is part of the Perfectly Imperfect exhibition at The Lavery, curated by Alex Tieghi-Walker. The exhibition also includes the second-ever Studio Iron collectible design show.

As London Design Festival (LDF) continues across the capital, there is still time to visit any or all of our must-see picks taking place until the end of the week.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture practice Studio Egret West has submitted a "more-permeable" masterplan for the final phases of the Battersea Power Station development in London.

Designed for the development's remaining 16-acre brownfield site, the updated masterplan by Studio Egret West would contain 3.2 million square feet of residential, commercial and leisure space.

The new proposal, which has been submitted by the studio for approval, updates the original 42-acre masterplan devised by Uruguayan architect Rafael Viñoly in 2008.

Viñoly's original design laid out plans for a mixed-use development centred around the grade II-listed Battersea Power Station, which was converted into housing, offices and commercial space by architecture studio WilkinsonEyre.

According to Studio Egret West, the newer plan was conceived in response to a public consultation that highlighted "major changes in urban living, working and how people spend their leisure time" since the project's inception.

"The revised masterplan builds on the success of the first half of the Battersea Power Station story, creating opportunities for more homes, workplaces, retail and leisure," studio co-founder David West said.

"The future phases will be more permeable, inclusive and intriguing, with an expanded network of playful, artistic and biodiverse public spaces."

"The refreshed vision is also deliberately flexible, leaving room for serendipity, while remaining responsive and resilient to what we've learned from the journey so far," West added.

Read:

Foster + Partners unveils curving office building at Battersea Power Station

Updates to the masterplan made by Studio Egret West include dividing the project's remaining phases into clusters of smaller buildings, connected by a network of streets and courtyards.

Renders of the proposal reveal a series of yet-to-be-detailed high-rise buildings, including homes, cultural venues and commercial spaces, interspersed with planted walkways and outdoor seating space.

A new green space has also been designed to connect the Battersea Power Station development with the wider Nine Elms area.

The plans also specify stronger visual connections between the new developments and the grade II-listed Battersea Power Station.

According to the studio, one phase of the project's future developments has already received planning permission to deliver 200 new council homes in partnership with Wandsworth Council.

More than 2,200 homes and around 800,000 square feet of office space have already been completed as part of the development. This includes a curving office building by Foster + Partners and a roof garden that tops a Foster + Partners-designed residential building with 23,000 plants.

The renders are by Studio Egret West.

item.content:encoded:
Designer Tom Pearson has created industrial furniture pieces with rivets that are both structural and decorative for the 10,000 Rivets collection, on show at APOC Store during London Design Festival.

The line, which is Tom Pearson Studio's debut furniture and lighting collection, is on show at London's APOC store, where the aluminium pieces function as display cases and tables for contemporary fashion.

Pearson, who previously co-founded and co-ran the fabrication workshop Jamps Studio, turned his focus to the modest industrial fixing for 10,000 Rivets.

He also explored different ways to create surface designs on the aluminium sheets through anodising – a process that changes the metal's structure near its surface and creates a water-resistant layer.

"The works came from wanting to further my experiments with anodising," Pearson told Dezeen. "The forms are driven by the constraints of the anodising process."

"The acid tanks I have can only accommodate a certain sheet size, and welding anodised aluminium is feasible but messy, hence the riveted construction," he continued.

"I think it's nicer to be led by chance and play than starting with an overarching 'concept'."

The designer started to play around with the anodising process because of the difficulties in finishing aluminium designs.

"Anyone who has worked with aluminium knows how much of a nightmare finishing is – you look away, and it's covered in fingerprints," he said.

Read:

Studio Iron exhibition is all about chainmail, cowhide and tattooed leather

"Anodising is the solution, but it's hard to find a supplier who is happy for you to experiment in the corner," Pearson continued.

"I started anodising parts myself because I wanted to apply the dyes by hand with brushes without aiming for the usual uniform flat colour."

While Pearson uses a traditional set-up for anodising aluminium, he experimented with different ways of applying dye to the material, using brushes, airbrushes and pipettes.

The resulting patterns look like water droplets, creating a surface design that is both unusual and decorative.

"My setup is no different to the usual process, involving acid and boiling water; I am just treating it as a decorative patina embracing all the unpredictability of the process," Pearson said.

Pearson's aluminium pieces, which have angular, geometric shapes, are held together by rivets that run along their seams.

This creates a look that makes some of the shelving seem as if it's floating, and gives the shelves, tables, accessories and lighting designs sculptural patterned edges.

While the pieces on show feature thousands of rivets, they do not quite make it to the number in the exhibition's name.

"There are technically 6,264 rivets in the works," Pearson said. "I ordered 10,000. Who knows where the rest have gone!"

Other London Design Festival projects on Dezeen include Studio Iron's show featuring chainmail, cowhide and tattooed leather and an exhibition designed as a fictional 1930s hotel suite.

The collection was produced by design consultancy Heavy Duty Services. The photography is by Studio Adamson.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: H World has debuted its latest hotel brand, the Grand Ji Hotel, in Hangzhou, China, designed by Chinese studio Vermilion Zhou Design Group, which aims to reinvent hotel design through its dedication to symbolic ritual.

Grand Ji Hotel, a premium brand under H World Group, has made its official debut at Paris Design Week's China Creative Power (CCP) pavilion as an official annual partner, taking place from 10 to 19 September.

The hotel's spatial design was led by Kuang Ming (Ray) Chou, founder and creative director of Vermilion Zhou Design Group and chief designer of H World Group.

According to H World, Grand Ji Hotel draws on the phrase "the formless greatness, a quiet way of seeing" and is informed by the Taoist concept of 大象无形, which suggests that the most powerful forms are often "quiet and insular".

Instead of an overtly luxurious look, the hotel's aesthetic is described as "quiet, yet possessed of presence, unlayered, yet full of depth".

Rather than weaving traditional Chinese imagery throughout the hotel design, Grand Ji Hotel was designed to break the conventional hotel paradigms and instead focus on quietly enhancing visitor experience.

For example, the way guests arrive, dine, rest and depart are treated as part of one integrated system.

When guests arrive, instead of checking in at a large front desk, they are greeted by a tea table where they can first enjoy a tea ceremony and a hot cup of tea.

At Grand Ji Hotels, technology is integrated purposefully into the background to ensure a smooth experience.

Visitors can use their phones as a room key, and rooms are also fitted with innovative control systems, where curtains, televisions, and air conditioning are controlled via voice commands.

H World explained that the "Eastern spirit" is woven into each room's design, with furniture that evokes a sense of sensory calm and hospitality rituals embedded in the structure.

Throughout the creative process, the designers also looked to incorporate cultural and natural motifs into the building's spatial qualities.

Here, the materials, art and how light flows through the building were influenced by five Eastern motifs: water, clouds, mountains, pine and tea.

Water symbolises the hotel's flow and calmness, clouds stand for lightness, tea represents zen, mountains signify depth, and pine embodies resilience.

H World explained that its inclusion in Paris Design Week is the first time a Chinese hotel brand has taken part in the week under its own name, which marks a shift from Chinese hotel brands "leading in scale" to "leading in design."

H World added that Grand Ji Hotel's participation also spotlights the Chinese hotel industry's growing force within the international design space.

With over 13,000 hotels and more than one million rooms across 21 countries, H World Group is one of the world's largest hotel groups.

The company is headquartered in Shanghai, China, and also offers a portfolio spanning diverse brands, including HanTing Hotel, JI Hotel, Orange Hotel, IntercityHotel, Zleep Hotel, Steigenberger Hotels & Resorts and Steigenberger Icons.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: subtly reflective silver-grey glass and tactile physical controls characterise Fisher & Paykel's Contemporary Style kitchen appliances, designed with versatility for the social heart of the home.

The Contemporary appliances are one of three product design styles in the New Zealand company's luxury range, alongside the Minimal and Professional offerings.

Fisher & Paykel explained that each of its curated styles supports architects, designers and homeowners in creating bespoke kitchens with a cohesive aesthetic.

"The advantage is a consistent design language across the appliance collection, from cooking and cooling to wine care and dishwashing," said the brand.

Fisher & Paykel's Contemporary Style includes flush-fitting ovens and cooktops as well as an expansive ecosystem of complementary appliances, all with the same focus on clean lines, softly silver surfaces and comfortable interaction.

Its aesthetic contrasts with the Minimal Style, where dark colours and dial- and handle-free designs allow the products to recede into the background.

Together, the style families are intended to enable the creation of bespoke spaces befitting the evolving role of the domestic kitchen.
Fisher & Paykel explained that once hidden from view, kitchens are now one of the main social spaces in the home.

They attract a constant thrum of activity as families join in meal preparation, guests hover and chat, and daily rituals are tended to.

Within this context, the brand's style families bring the "beauty of choice" to architects, designers and homeowners in the luxury market, letting them pick products for both their function and cohesion with a material palette.

For the Contemporary range, Fisher & Paykel focused on a timeless appearance, with clean lines and tonal contrasts. Knowledge of interaction and how people experience the space was also taken into consideration.

The brushed silver glass on the ovens has an "active relationship with its surroundings", said the company, picking up on the tones of surrounding materials like stone and timber and gently shifting its appearance as the light changes throughout the day.

"The silver-grey glass finish was designed to create depth and subtle reflectivity within the kitchen," said Fisher & Paykel head of industrial design (cooking) Adam Moody.

"As light changes throughout the day, the products reveal different qualities and relationships with surrounding materials."

The Contemporary range is intended to complement both light and dark interiors, either adding contrast and depth through reflectivity
in darker spaces, or reading softly against pale cabinetry, tile and stone.

"With Contemporary Style, we wanted to create a refined material presence: expressive enough to add depth and character to the kitchen, but restrained enough to work across a wide range of architectural interiors," added Moody.

Fisher & Paykel marries these finishes with precisely machined dials, round bar handles that sit comfortably in the hand and carefully calibrated door movement, emphasising tactility.

This is complemented with intuitive touchscreens and SmartHQ app connectivity for detailed and remote control.

The Contemporary line includes steam, convection and combination ovens as well as companion products such as vacuum seal drawers and warming drawers.

Gas or induction hobs are also available, with stainless steel or black glass finishes. Refrigerators, wine cabinets, range cookers, cooker hoods and dishwashers complete the offering.

The Contemporary Style products are designed for flush-fit installation and sit precisely within cabinetry, with only fine gaps as small as two millimetres. There are 60- and 76-centimetre formats to suit different layouts.

Fisher & Paykel was founded in New Zealand in 1934. Find out more about the company and its Contemporary Style luxury appliances on its website.

Dezeen Showroom: from glossy to stone-effect tiles, Italian manufacturer Marazzi has listed a handful of its versatile products on Dezeen Showroom.

Mystone Pietra di Sicilia tiles are made from porcelain, yet evoke the warmth and tactility of stones mined in Sicily.

Subtle striations and veining run across the tiles, recalling the natural variations found in limestone and marble.

A trio of neutral finishes are available, alongside a plethora of different size formats.

Mystone Tivoli tiles are named and designed after Tivoli stone, a travertine marble often used in the construction of ancient Roman architecture.

Regardless of size format or colour, the tiles can be used indoors or out for various purposes, from paving to cladding.

Ridged clay-coloured detailing creates visual interest in the brand's Terramater tiles, made from a combination of specialised surface glazing and porcelain stoneware for the body of the tile.

Seven colourways and two surface patterns are available: linear Ritmo and lozenge-shaped Losanga.

Marazzi used its 3D ink technology to create dramatic and realistic striations that run through its Mystone Silver Root tiles.

The brand aims for this to be indistinguishable from natural quarried stone, with the hygiene benefits of porcelain tiles.

The brand has expanded its zellige-style Lume tile collection so that it now features a 10-by-10-centimetre square tile.

Neutral and vivid colourways can be chosen from, as well as a new style tile called Dew, which subtly recalls the shape of a leaf.

Marazzi was founded in 1935 and specialises in the sourcing, design and production of tiles intended for use across residential projects, commercial settings and hospitality interiors.

The Italian brand uses longstanding design and manufacturing techniques in an effort to preserve local tile-making traditions.

item.content:encoded:
Canadian studio RHAD Architects has completed Two Bay House in Nova Scotia, Canada, which consists of blocky volumes with carved-out voids, mass-timber framing and blackened wood cladding.

The waterfront home is located within a family estate on Cape Breton Island, in northeastern Nova Scotia.

The design began with two simple masses, which were then strategically carved away to form courtyards, terraces and double-height spaces.  These voids were designed to "mediate between shelter and landscape".

"The architecture emerges not through the addition of elements, but through a series of deliberate acts of subtraction and carving," said RHAD Architects, a studio based in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, and led by founder Rayleen Hill.

"The resulting voids are as significant as the forms themselves, becoming the spaces through which the house is experienced."

The house rises two levels and is partly made of mass timber. Its primary roof structure consists of glue-laminated timber, while the roof decking is standard lumber.

The walls are made of insulated concrete forms (ICFs).

In plan, it consists of two parallel bars, or "bays", with one shorter in length.

"Their differing lengths establish a protected, west-facing courtyard that shelters outdoor living from prevailing waterfront winds while capturing afternoon sunlight," the team said.

Exterior walls are clad in vertical wooden siding that was charred using shou sugi ban (yakisugi), an ancient Japanese technique. Treated with black oil, the burnt wood "gives the building a quiet, monolithic presence within the landscape".

In carved-away areas, the solid charred wood gives way to slatted wood and vertical-grain hemlock siding.

"The contrast between charred and natural wood makes each subtraction legible, revealing the spaces where the architecture opens itself to light, landscape and occupation," the team said.

The home is entered on the east, where one finds an entry court enclosed within tall, slatted walls.

Filtered sunlight passes into the threshold, creating changing patterns throughout the day, while the enclosure glows in the evening from internal light.

The vertical space acts as a "constant point of reference" within the home, the team said.

Inside, there is a division between communal and private areas.

The shorter of the two volumes contains two bedrooms on the bottom level and a primary bedroom up above.

The longer volume holds a kitchen, dining area and living room on the ground floor. Upstairs, there is a music room and a small salon, as one of the clients is a hairstylist.

A large portion of the upper floor is carved away, forming a void in the centre of the house. A loft and glass-walled bridge overlook the communal area, "allowing light, conversation and activity to move freely between levels".

Along the water-facing side of the house, ample glazing and covered terraces extend the interior living spaces outward – "allowing the architecture to project into the landscape while maintaining a strong sense of enclosure", the team said.

The west side of the house features a swimming pool surrounded by a generous terrace.

Overall, it was designed to show "how subtraction can generate richness," the studio said.

 

"Rather than relying on formal complexity, it demonstrates how carefully carved voids can produce moments of compression and release, darkness and light, intimacy and openness.

"The result is a home whose character is defined as much by the spaces removed as by those that remain."

Other homes in Nova Scotia include a cedar-wrapped house by Omar Gandhi Architects that sits on a rocky coastline, and a residence by MacKay-Lyons Sweetapple that is a "village" of gabled steel structures.

The photography is by Adrian Ozimek.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio HKS has unveiled interior designs for the upcoming Washington Commanders NFL stadium in Washington DC, showing what its glass ceiling will look like.

The renderings showcase a steep bowl underneath the glass ceiling, giving fans an idea of the much-anticipated 70,000-seat stadium ahead of its construction.

Noteworthy is the continuous ring of stands, designed without the interruption from protruding box seats or the overhangs typical of most NFL-sized stadiums.

HKS architect Aaron Hollis said that the priority was a unified viewing experience for fans.

"We designed this bowl from the inside out, starting with a single question: what should it feel like when every fan is part of the game?" said Hollis.

"Every decision, from the steepness of the seating to the elimination of overhangs, was driven by that question. The result is a single, unified bowl where nothing separates the fans from the action or from each other."

Digital banners are shown running around select tiers, with a large banner wrapping the top of the stadium. In some images, the digital banners are shown reflecting off the glass ceiling.

When the initial exterior renderings were announced, HKS emphasised its intention to design both deferentially and referentially to the architecture of the US capital.

Read:

Four upcoming NFL stadiums that show the future of the league

This principle seems to have continued on the inside – the stands open up at one end to directly frame the dome of the US Capitol building.

The design of the bowl was informed by RFK Stadium, which is being demolished to make way for the HKS design.

HKS also emphasised the loudness of the design and said the elements work together "to capture crowd noise inside the stadium and push it back down toward the field".

"The result: one of the loudest stadiums in the NFL," said the studio.

The stadium design has become a national talking point. Earlier this year, an aide to US president Donald Trump suggested the stadium should be "classical" in line with the administration's executive order giving precedent to the style across federal buildings.

The stadium's site near the Anacostia River is administered by local government and falls outside of the mandate. Still, the architecture studio integrated columns on the exterior that are modern in form but capture some elements of classical ornamentation.

The Washington Commanders Stadium at the RFK Campus is set to open around 2030.

The images are courtesy of the Washington Commanders.

item.content:encoded:
Austrian studio Lechner & Lechner Architects has added an annexe clad in charred timber to a house in the Alps, designed as a minimalist space to "withdraw and think".

Named Quiet Retreat, the pared-back annexe sits as a standalone multipurpose room alongside an existing home in Salzkammergut, Austria, creating a loosely U-shaped ensemble around a central patio.

Lechner & Lechner Architects designed the space to feel "open but never exposed", with a wall of foldable glass doors along one edge overlooking woodland, a rocky outcrop and expansive views across meadows and the Alps in the distance.

"The landscape was really the starting point of the project," studio partner Paul Lechner told Dezeen.

"The existing rock and the building form a kind of natural atrium on a small rise. From there, the space opens towards the meadows and the surrounding mountains," added Lechner.

"We wanted the house to feel open to the landscape, but never exposed. Finding that balance was something we worked on throughout the design process," he added.

Read:

Mossy rooftop crowns Bather's Cabin in East Sussex woodland

The space has been purposefully left free of any fitted elements that would suggest a specific purpose, save for a series of climbing holds on one of its walls and a traditional Alpine bell hung from the ceiling.

A single window at one end of the annexe frames views of the adjacent forest, while on the long edge of the space folding glass doors open the interior up to a gravel patio sheltered by the rocky outcrop.

"Rather than separating different activities into individual rooms, the space is used as a place for creative work, writing, playing and simply spending time there," Lechner said. "It is also a quiet place to withdraw and think."

Atop a slim concrete base, the dark, charred-timber cladding of Quiet Retreat was chosen as a nod to traditional black Alpine barns, and achieved using the Japanese technique of Shou Sugi Ban.

To create contrast in the interiors, the walls and gabled ceiling are entirely lined in pale panels of oriented strand board (OSB).

"The contrast between the dark exterior and the lighter interior became an important part of the character of the house," Lechner told Dezeen. "There is also a connection to Alpine building traditions, where timber facades naturally become darker, greyer and more weathered over time."

"By charring the timber, the building does not have this very new appearance at the beginning. It feels more settled in the landscape from day one," he added.

Other projects in the Austrian Alps recently featured on Dezeen include the renovation of a 17th-century Alpine lodge into a boutique hotel by owners and architects Gerold and Katia Schneider, and a shingle-clad viewing tower on a mountain peak by Snøhetta.

The photography is by Julian Höck.

item.content:encoded:
Artist Isamaya Ffrench has opened her second-ever Studio Iron show as part of this year's London Design Festival, with participants including Andu Masebo and Barnaby Lewis.

Studio Iron is the brainchild of Ffrench, a makeup artist and creative director, who launched her collectible design gallery at Saatchi Yates earlier this year.

The project is back for London Design Festival (LDF), on display as part of curator Alex Tieghi-Walker's Perfectly Imperfect programme in the Brompton Design District.

Ffrench selected 27 creatives for the exhibition, featuring pieces that challenge ideas about what materials go together.

"Our designers are based all over the world, and as someone who's highly into the tactility of objects and art, it was amazing to see all the pieces in real life," she told Dezeen. "To see how they looked, what they felt like, and to witness their scale."

"Most of the time, we get to experience art and design on the internet, in museums or in shops as the finished piece with great lighting and great props," she continued.

"But I'm more interested in the process, the tools, the raw materials, and the industrial machines. It's a real privilege to be in an artist's space and to talk to them about their inspiration or see them at work."

Among the selection is a low-slung hammered steel pouf by Jesse Butterfield, topped with a lacy linen cushion by Jane Wright.

Opposite the pouf, an oversized, angular armchair by tattoo artist Thomas Cardiff is on display, crafted from a steel frame with a cowhide-clad seat and tattooed leather sides.

Marten Herma Anderson is showing a bloated resin lamp with a gridded pattern and a nickel-plated brass base, while Atelier Fomenta is presenting a bulb encased in a cylindrical slab of rubber held together with rivets.

A tangled stainless steel coat rack by Andu Masebo was placed in the corner of the gallery, close to a chunky hammered steel mirror, also by Butterfield.

Blacksmith Barnaby Lewis's spindly, skeletal chair features in the show, alongside a stainless steel floor lamp by Wretched Flowers, cloaked in chainmail, gemstones and glass beads.

Lewis is among the London-based rising talents spotlighted in the Dezeen Dispatch newspaper we published for LDF.

"Barnaby's practice is visceral and poetic at the same time and he's also wildly prolific," Ffrench told Dezeen. "His work deserves more attention."

Read:

London has "the best architecture and interior design community in Europe" says Duncan Riches

London-based Ffrench said that she hopes to expand Studio Iron, which is still in its infancy, into an interdisciplinary creative agency that champions young designers.

"London feels genuinely open in terms of how people work," said the artist. "There's less pressure to attach yourself to a single practice, which makes it easier to move between disciplines."

"Galleries and shops are also much more inclined to represent and sell the work of emerging artists versus established ones," added Ffrench. "And I think it is vital to support them and help them grow."

LDF is in full swing in the UK capital, with current shows ranging from a lighting installation by Lee Broom to the launch of prototype furniture and object platform Lobby.

The photography is by Andy Stagg.

The Studio Iron show is on show from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Dezeen Showroom: 1970s-style curves meet creative textural contrast in the Nina lounge chair, designed by Patricia Urquiola for furniture brand Andreu World.

The Nina lounge chair has a bulbous, organic shape that looks almost pebble-like from the front, which flows in a continuous, looping curve around itself, forming a sculptural back.

Andreu World says the shape was inspired by the 1656 Diego Velázquez painting Las Meninas, where the subjects wear oversized, enveloping crinolines, as well as paying homage to the "expressive freedom" of 1970s furniture.

Instead of being entirely upholstered, the chair features gentle juxtaposition from a hard structural back shell made of the Spanish brand's Pure ECO thermopolymer, produced from 100 per cent recycled polymer waste.

This shell is available in a glossy or matt enamel finish and features a pockmarked organic relief reminiscent of stone. Inspired by surfaces shaped by water, it brings extra personality to the already commanding chair.

Made from high-quality technical foams and carefully tailored upholstery, Patricia Urquiola intended for the Nina lounge chair to be used in both residential and professional environments, where its wide, armless seat invites easy repose.

item.content:encoded:
A land reclamation project has added the equivalent of 42 football pitches to Denmark's southern coast, as part of the construction of the Fehmarnbelt Tunnel under the Baltic Sea.

Fehmarnbelt Tunnel is an 18-kilometre-long road-and-rail tunnel, set to be the longest of its kind in the world. It is being built to connect Denmark and Germany and improve links between continental Europe and Scandinavia.

Seabed excavations from the project have been repurposed as an artificial island measuring approximately 300,000 square metres on the coast of Rødbyhavn, which is set to be landscaped as a nature spot.

"People can experience distinctive coastal nature"

State-owned transport company Sund & Bælt, which is developing the project, said the land will "become a unique experience for visitors".

“We have reused material from the seabed to create an area where people can experience distinctive coastal nature, with walking trails, ponds and wildlife including birds, amphibians and insects," said project manager Ditte Hjort.

"What makes the new area so special is that visitors can follow nature’s development right from the outset. We hope it will become a unique experience for visitors, with salt marshes and rich, diverse wildlife and plant life."

The 18-kilometre tunnel is being built to connect Rødbyhavn in Denmark with Puttgarden in Germany, and is scheduled for completion in 2029.

It will be formed of 89 concrete elements,, measuring 217 metres in length and 73,000 tonnes in weight, which will be submerged and combined in a man-made trench in the seabed.

It is expected to reduce journey times between Hamburg and Copenhagen to 2.5 hours by train.

Native plants will cover the land

The 300,000 square metres of land that has been added to Denmark as part of the project is set to be landscaped with three ponds and planting to withstand harsh coastal climate.

Soil that was excavated to build a factory from the tunnel has also been spread across the site, containing plant seeds that are hoped to bring life to the new landscape.

Read:

Artificial island Lynetteholm to be built in Copenhagen harbour

An agreement between Denmark and Germany to build the tunnel was signed in 2008, but delays followed due to opposition from ferry operators and conservation groups.

Elsewhere in Denmark, an artificial island called Lynetteholm is currently under development off the coast of Copenhagen to house 35,000 people and act as a defence against rising sea levels.

Architecture studio Urban Power is also designing nine artificial islands, named Holmene, off the coast of the city that will become a sustainable tech hub.
